slides.title: Probability Foundations
slides.subtitle: From sample spaces to conditional reasoning

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.outcome: By the end of this lecture, students should be able to:
objectives: Define a sample space and represent events as subsets.
Distinguish mutually exclusive events from independent events.
Apply addition, multiplication, and conditional-probability rules.
Interpret Bayes' theorem as an update from prior to posterior belief.
Solve and explain a probability problem using a structured workflow.

slides.title: Building a Probability Model
slides.subtitle: Every correct calculation starts with a clearly defined experiment, outcome, and event.

content.lead: A probability model describes every outcome that can occur and the events we care about.
content.body: The sample space Ω contains all possible outcomes. An event is any subset of Ω. The quality of the model depends on whether the outcomes are complete, non-overlapping, and expressed at the right level of detail.
bullets: Outcome: one possible result of the experiment
Sample space: the complete set of possible outcomes
Event: a collection of outcomes that answers a question
Complement: every outcome that is not in the event
content.definition: An event is a subset of the sample space.
content.example: For one die roll, A = {2, 4, 6} represents an even result.

slides.title: Translate the Story Before You Calculate

content.lead: Probability problems are easier when the narrative is converted into explicit events.
content.body: Underline the experiment, list the possible outcomes, name the relevant events, and only then select a rule.
bullets: State what is random and what is fixed
Choose event labels that match the question
Check whether order and replacement matter

visual.caption: A clear model connects the wording of a problem to its mathematical structure.
visual.alt: Open textbook used as a visual metaphor for translating a written problem

left.title: Mutually Exclusive
left.subtitle: The events cannot occur together.
points: One event rules out the other
Example: one die roll is 2 and 5
Usually not independent when both have positive probability

right.title: Independent
right.subtitle: Knowing one event occurred does not change the other.
points: Information about A does not change P(B)
Example: outcomes of two separate fair coin flips

process.title: Define
process.body: Name the random experiment and the target event.

process.title: Represent
process.body: Use a list, tree, table, or diagram to organize outcomes.

process.title: Select
process.body: Choose the rule that matches the event relationship.

process.title: Calculate
process.body: Substitute values and keep intermediate steps visible.

process.title: Interpret
process.body: Explain the result in the language of the original problem.

slides.title: How the Main Probability Ideas Connect

nodes.title: Random Experiment
nodes.body: A repeatable process with uncertain output

rows: The event is easier to describe by what does not happen
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
At least one of two events occurs
The sample space is restricted by B
P(B) must be greater than zero

equation.label: Definition
equation.explanation: The numerator counts outcomes in both A and B; the denominator restricts attention to outcomes in B.

bullets: Read P(A | B) as probability of A given B
Treat B as the new sample space
The order of A and B matters

slides.title: Bayes' Theorem Is a Rearrangement of Joint Probability

steps.explanation: Write the multiplication rule with B as the condition.
Write the same joint event with A as the condition.
Set the two expressions for the same joint probability equal.
Divide by P(B) to isolate the posterior probability.

slides.title: Quality Control: Probability of a Defective Item

problem.statement: A production line makes 240 items and 12 are defective. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected item is defective.
problem.final_answer: The estimated probability of selecting a defective item is 0.05, or 5%.

problem.statement: A card is drawn from a standard deck. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
problem.hint: The king of hearts belongs to both events, so count the overlap only once.

slides.title: Build a Probability Model from a Short Scenario

activity.task: Model the outcomes of selecting two students from a group and decide whether order matters.
instructions: Define the experiment and state any assumptions.
Choose labels for the relevant events.
Represent the outcomes using a table or tree.
Write one probability question that can be answered from your model.
Exchange models with another pair and check for missing outcomes.
activity.deliverable: One labeled representation and one justified probability calculation

slides.title: Case Study: A Screening Test with Rare Prevalence

case_study.context: A screening program tests a population in which only 1% of people have the condition.
case_study.challenge: The test has high sensitivity, yet many positive results may still be false positives because the condition is rare.
case_study.evidence: Students receive sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence values and must organize them in a 2×2 table.
questions: Which probability represents the positive predictive value?
Why does prevalence change the interpretation of a positive result?

quote.text: A probability is not just a number; it is a statement about a model, its assumptions, and the information currently available.
quote.author: Lecture takeaway

points: Define the sample space before selecting a probability rule.
Mutually exclusive and independent describe different relationships.
Conditional probability changes the reference set.
Bayes' theorem combines prior knowledge with new evidence.
A complete solution includes interpretation, not only arithmetic.
summary.takeaway: Model the event relationship first; the correct formula usually follows.
